q: During nasotracheal intubation, the tube is passed along the floor of the nose. Which structure forms most of the lateral wall of the nasal cavity that the tube must avoid?
why: The lateral wall carries the three turbinates (conchae) with their meatuses. Passing the tube along the nasal floor, below the inferior turbinate, reduces turbinate trauma and bleeding. The septum is the medial wall, the cribriform plate the roof and the hard palate the floor.

q: Which sinus or duct drains into the inferior meatus of the nose?
why: The nasolacrimal duct opens into the inferior meatus. The frontal, maxillary and anterior ethmoidal sinuses drain into the middle meatus (hiatus semilunaris), the posterior ethmoidal cells into the superior meatus, and the sphenoid sinus into the sphenoethmoidal recess.

q: Which muscle is the only one that abducts the vocal cords?
why: Posterior cricoarytenoid is the sole abductor. Lateral cricoarytenoid and the arytenoids adduct; cricothyroid tenses the cords (external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve); thyroarytenoid relaxes them. All except cricothyroid are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

q: Sensation to the laryngeal mucosa above the vocal cords is supplied by which nerve?
o: External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
why: The internal laryngeal nerve pierces the thyrohyoid membrane to supply sensation above the cords (and is blocked at the greater horn of the hyoid for awake intubation). The recurrent laryngeal supplies sensation below the cords. The glossopharyngeal supplies the posterior third of the tongue and oropharynx.

q: Why is an inhaled foreign body in an adult more likely to enter the right main bronchus?
o: The carina lies to the right of the midline
The right bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical
The right bronchus is longer and narrower
The right lung has fewer segments
The left bronchus is guarded by the aortic arch valve
why: The right main bronchus is about 2.5 cm long, wider and leaves at about 25° from vertical; the left is about 5 cm, narrower and at about 45°, passing under the aortic arch. The right upper lobe bronchus arises within 2.5 cm of the carina, which matters for right-sided double-lumen tubes.

q: How many bronchopulmonary segments does the right lung typically have?
why: The right lung has 10 segments: upper lobe 3 (apical, posterior, anterior), middle lobe 2 (lateral, medial), lower lobe 5 (superior, medial, anterior, lateral and posterior basal). The left has 8–10 depending on whether apicoposterior and anteromedial segments are counted as fused.

q: Which cell produces surfactant in the alveolus?
why: Type II pneumocytes (cuboidal, about 5% of surface area) secrete surfactant (mainly dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine) and act as progenitors for type I cells. Type I cells are thin and cover about 95% of the alveolar surface for gas exchange. Club cells line the bronchioles.

q: What is the approximate thickness of the alveolar–capillary barrier at its thinnest point?
why: The blood–gas barrier (type I cell, fused basement membranes and endothelium) is about 0.2–0.5 µm thick over a surface area of 50–100 m², which suits rapid diffusion according to Fick's law.

q: Which structure lies in the posterior mediastinum?
why: The posterior mediastinum contains the descending aorta, oesophagus, thoracic duct, azygos and hemiazygos veins and the sympathetic chains (alongside). The thymus is in the anterior (and superior) mediastinum; the heart, pericardium, ascending aorta and phrenic nerves are in the middle mediastinum.

q: The boundary between the superior and inferior mediastinum is a plane passing through which level?
o: The manubriosternal angle and the T4/T5 disc
why: The transverse thoracic plane runs from the angle of Louis to the T4/5 intervertebral disc. At this level the aortic arch begins and ends, the trachea bifurcates, the azygos enters the SVC and the second costal cartilage articulates.

q: Compared with an adult, which feature describes the neonatal airway?
o: The trachea is relatively long and narrow
The epiglottis is short, broad and stiff
The cricoid ring is the narrowest fixed point
The tongue is relatively small for the mouth
The larynx sits lower, at C5–C6
why: Neonates have a larynx at about C3–C4, a long floppy U-shaped epiglottis, a relatively large tongue and occiput, and a short trachea (about 4–5 cm). The subglottis at the cricoid has traditionally been described as the narrowest point; MRI studies suggest the glottis is narrowest but the cricoid ring is non-distensible.

q: Why is a neonate's diaphragm more prone to fatigue than an adult's?
o: It has no central tendon at birth
It has fewer fatigue-resistant type I fibres
It is innervated by C2–C3 roots only
It inserts higher on more vertical ribs
why: The neonatal diaphragm has about 25% type I fibres (about 55% in adults), its ribs are horizontal and the chest wall is compliant, so the work of breathing is high and fatigue occurs early, particularly in preterm infants.

q: The cricothyroid membrane is identified for emergency front-of-neck access. What lies immediately superior to it?
why: The cricothyroid membrane lies between the inferior border of the thyroid cartilage and the superior border of the cricoid cartilage. The thyroid isthmus usually lies over tracheal rings 2–4, so it is below the membrane. DAS recommends the laryngeal handshake to locate it.

q: During laryngoscopy with a Macintosh blade, where is the blade tip placed?
o: In the vallecula, anterior to the epiglottis
In the piriform fossa beside the larynx
Posterior to the epiglottis, lifting it directly
why: The curved Macintosh blade tip sits in the vallecula; lifting tensions the hyoepiglottic ligament, which elevates the epiglottis indirectly. A straight (Miller) blade lifts the epiglottis directly, which is helpful in infants with a long floppy epiglottis.

q: Which cardiac valve has three cusps named anterior, posterior and septal?
why: The tricuspid valve has anterior, posterior and septal leaflets. The mitral valve has anterior and posterior leaflets. The aortic valve has right, left and non-coronary (posterior) cusps; the pulmonary valve has anterior, left and right cusps.

q: Which chamber forms most of the anterior (sternocostal) surface of the heart?
why: The right ventricle forms most of the sternocostal surface. The left ventricle forms the apex and most of the left border and diaphragmatic surface; the left atrium forms most of the base (posterior surface), lying close to the oesophagus, which is why TOE images it well.

q: In a right-dominant coronary circulation, which artery gives rise to the posterior descending artery?
why: Dominance is defined by which artery supplies the posterior descending artery. About 70–80% of people are right dominant (RCA), around 10% left dominant (circumflex) and the remainder co-dominant.

q: Which coronary artery most commonly supplies the sinoatrial node?
why: The SA nodal artery arises from the RCA in about 60% and from the circumflex in about 40%. The AV node is supplied by the artery that gives the posterior descending artery (usually the RCA), so inferior MI often causes heart block.

q: What is the main physiological purpose of the delay at the atrioventricular node?
o: To protect the SA node from overdrive pacing
To let atrial systole finish ventricular filling
To synchronise contraction of papillary muscles
To lengthen the QT interval and refractoriness
To prevent retrograde conduction to the atria
why: Slow conduction through the AV node (about 0.1 s, giving much of the PR interval) allows atrial systole to finish filling the ventricles before they contract. It also limits ventricular rate during atrial tachyarrhythmias.

q: Which part of the conducting system has the fastest conduction velocity?
why: Purkinje fibres conduct at about 2–4 m/s, allowing near-simultaneous ventricular activation. The AV node is slowest (about 0.05 m/s); atrial muscle and the bundle of His conduct at about 1 m/s.

q: Which is the first branch of the aortic arch?
why: The arch gives the brachiocephalic trunk, then the left common carotid, then the left subclavian. The brachiocephalic divides behind the right sternoclavicular joint into the right subclavian and right common carotid arteries.

q: Which nerve hooks under the aortic arch, explaining left vocal cord palsy with aortic arch aneurysms?
why: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the arch near the ligamentum arteriosum and ascends in the tracheo-oesophageal groove. The right recurrent nerve loops under the right subclavian artery. A large left atrium or arch aneurysm can compress the left nerve (Ortner's syndrome).

q: The anterior cerebral artery supplies which territory?
o: Lateral surface of the frontal and parietal lobes
Medial surface of the frontal and parietal lobes
why: The ACA supplies the medial frontal and parietal cortex, so occlusion causes contralateral leg weakness and sensory loss. The MCA supplies most of the lateral cortex (face and arm, language in the dominant hemisphere); the PCA supplies the occipital lobe.

q: The two vertebral arteries unite to form which vessel?
why: The vertebral arteries ascend through the foramina transversaria of C6–C1, enter via the foramen magnum and join at the pontomedullary junction to form the basilar artery, which divides into the two posterior cerebral arteries.

sb: Lower Limb Nerve Supply — Lumbar & Sacral Plexus
q: Which nerve roots form the femoral nerve?
why: The femoral nerve arises from the posterior divisions of L2–L4; the obturator nerve from the anterior divisions of L2–L4. The sciatic nerve arises from L4–S3 and the pudendal from S2–S4.

sb: Lower Limb Nerve Supply — Lumbar & Sacral Plexus
q: Which nerve supplies sensation to the medial side of the leg down to the medial malleolus?
why: The saphenous nerve is the terminal sensory branch of the femoral nerve. It supplies the medial leg and ankle, which is why a sciatic or popliteal block alone does not give complete analgesia below the knee.

q: Kiesselbach's plexus (Little's area), the commonest site of epistaxis, lies on which part of the nose?
why: Little's area on the anteroinferior septum is an anastomosis of the anterior ethmoidal, sphenopalatine, greater palatine and superior labial (facial) arteries. Posterior bleeds usually arise from sphenopalatine branches.

q: Which artery is the main arterial supply to the nasal cavity?
why: The sphenopalatine artery, a terminal branch of the maxillary artery (external carotid), is the main supply. The anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries come from the ophthalmic artery (internal carotid); the facial artery contributes via the superior labial artery.

q: What is the motor nerve supply to most muscles of the pharynx?
why: The pharyngeal constrictors and most palatal muscles are supplied by the vagus via the pharyngeal plexus. The exceptions are stylopharyngeus (glossopharyngeal) and tensor veli palatini (mandibular division of trigeminal).

q: At which vertebral level does the pharynx become the oesophagus in an adult?
why: The pharynx ends and the oesophagus begins at the lower border of the cricoid cartilage, at C6, where cricopharyngeus forms the upper oesophageal sphincter. The larynx also becomes the trachea at C6.

q: Which laryngeal cartilage is the only complete ring?
why: The cricoid is the only complete cartilaginous ring in the airway, shaped like a signet ring (taller posteriorly). This is why cricoid pressure can compress the oesophagus against C6, and why it limits tube size in children.

q: Damage to the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve during thyroidectomy causes which deficit?
o: Loss of sensation below the cords
Aspiration from loss of the cough reflex
Weak voice with loss of high pitch
why: The external laryngeal nerve, running with the superior thyroid artery, supplies cricothyroid, which tenses the cords. Injury causes a weak voice that cannot reach high pitch. Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury causes stridor.

sb: The Neck (Root of Neck at C6)
q: Which structure lies at the level of C6?
o: Upper border of the thyroid cartilage
why: At C6 lie the cricoid cartilage, the start of the trachea and oesophagus, the carotid (Chassaignac's) tubercle, where the vertebral artery enters the foramen transversarium and the middle cervical ganglion. The hyoid is at C3 and the carotid bifurcation at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage (C4).

sb: The Neck (Root of Neck at C6)
q: The stellate ganglion lies anterior to which structure?
o: The neck of the first rib
why: The stellate ganglion (fused inferior cervical and first thoracic ganglia) lies anterior to the neck of the first rib and the C7 transverse process, near the vertebral artery and pleural dome. It is commonly blocked at C6 (Chassaignac's tubercle) with spread downwards.

q: At which vertebral level does the oesophagus pass through the diaphragm?
why: Remember 'I 8 10 eggs at 12': IVC at T8 (with the right phrenic nerve), oesophagus at T10 (with the vagal trunks), aorta at T12 (with the thoracic duct and azygos vein).

q: What is the motor nerve supply to the diaphragm?
why: Motor supply is entirely from the phrenic nerves (C3, 4, 5). The peripheral diaphragm receives sensory fibres from the lower intercostal nerves. Interscalene blocks almost always block the ipsilateral phrenic nerve, causing hemidiaphragmatic paresis.

q: In an adult, where does the epidural space end inferiorly?
why: The epidural space extends from the foramen magnum (where the dura fuses with the periosteum) to the sacrococcygeal membrane at the sacral hiatus. The dural sac ends at about S2 and the spinal cord at about L1–L2 in adults.

q: Which ligament is the last to be traversed before entering the epidural space in the midline approach?
why: Midline order: skin, subcutaneous tissue, supraspinous ligament, interspinous ligament, ligamentum flavum, epidural space. The ligamentum flavum gives the characteristic resistance before loss of resistance. The posterior longitudinal ligament lies on the front wall of the canal.

q: Which vertebra has a long, usually non-bifid spinous process that is the most prominent palpable spine at the base of the neck?
why: C7 (vertebra prominens) has the longest cervical spinous process, usually not bifid, and is a key surface landmark. Typical cervical vertebrae (C3–C6) have bifid spines and foramina transversaria; at C7 the foramen usually transmits only vertebral veins.

q: Tuffier's line, joining the iliac crests, crosses the spine at approximately which level?
why: The intercristal line usually crosses L4 or the L4/5 interspace, though clinical estimates are often one space too high. Spinals are performed below L1–L2 to avoid the conus medullaris.

q: Which landmarks form the sacral hiatus used for caudal block?
why: The sacral hiatus results from failed fusion of the S5 (and sometimes S4) laminae and is bordered by the sacral cornua. It is covered by the sacrococcygeal ligament. The hiatus and the PSIS form an approximately equilateral triangle.

q: In a neonate, where does the dural sac usually end?
why: In neonates the dural sac ends at about S3–S4 (adults S2) and the spinal cord at about L3 (adults L1–L2), so the needle should be advanced only a few millimetres beyond the sacrococcygeal ligament during caudal block.

q: Which structure passes through the jugular foramen?
why: The jugular foramen transmits CN IX, X and XI and the internal jugular vein (sigmoid sinus). The hypoglossal nerve passes through the hypoglossal canal, the facial nerve through the internal acoustic meatus, and the mandibular nerve through foramen ovale.

q: Through which foramen does the maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve leave the skull?
why: V1 (ophthalmic) passes through the superior orbital fissure, V2 (maxillary) through foramen rotundum and V3 (mandibular) through foramen ovale. Foramen spinosum transmits the middle meningeal artery; the stylomastoid foramen transmits the facial nerve.

q: Which vessel connects the internal carotid artery to the posterior cerebral artery in the circle of Willis?
why: The posterior communicating arteries link the carotid and vertebrobasilar systems. The anterior communicating artery links the two anterior cerebral arteries and is the commonest site of berry aneurysm. A complete textbook circle is present in under half of people.

q: An aneurysm of the posterior communicating artery classically compresses which cranial nerve?
why: The oculomotor nerve passes between the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries, close to the posterior communicating artery. Compression gives a painful third nerve palsy with a dilated pupil (parasympathetic fibres lie superficially).

q: The sciatic nerve leaves the pelvis through which opening?
why: The sciatic nerve (L4–S3) usually exits through the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis, descending between the greater trochanter and ischial tuberosity. The superior gluteal nerve and vessels pass above piriformis.

q: Where does the sciatic nerve usually divide into the tibial and common peroneal nerves?
o: At the apex of the popliteal fossa
why: The division usually occurs at or just above the apex of the popliteal fossa (about 5–10 cm above the crease), though it is variable and can occur high in the pelvis. The popliteal block targets the nerve before or at the bifurcation.

q: At the level of the interscalene groove, the brachial plexus is organised as which component?
why: Roots emerge between scalenus anterior and medius and form trunks at the interscalene level. Divisions lie behind the clavicle, cords around the axillary artery (infraclavicular), and terminal branches in the axilla.

q: Which nerve arises from the posterior cord of the brachial plexus?
why: The posterior cord gives the radial and axillary nerves (plus subscapular and thoracodorsal nerves). The lateral cord gives the musculocutaneous and lateral root of the median; the medial cord gives the ulnar, medial root of the median and medial cutaneous nerves.

q: The superficial cervical plexus emerges at which surface landmark?
o: Angle of the mandible below the ear lobe
Suprasternal notch between the sternal heads
Anterior border of trapezius at the level of C7
Midpoint of the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid
Midpoint of the clavicle over the subclavian artery
why: The superficial branches (lesser occipital, great auricular, transverse cervical and supraclavicular nerves, C2–C4) emerge at Erb's point, the midpoint of the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid, where a superficial cervical plexus block is performed.

q: Which nerve arises from the cervical plexus and supplies motor fibres to the diaphragm?
why: The phrenic nerve (C3–C5) is the main motor branch of the deep cervical plexus, running on scalenus anterior. A deep cervical plexus block therefore commonly causes phrenic palsy, so bilateral deep blocks are avoided.

q: Where is most cerebrospinal fluid produced?
why: About 70% of CSF is produced by the choroid plexus, the rest by ependyma and brain interstitium, at about 500 mL/day (0.35 mL/min). Total volume is about 150 mL. It is absorbed mainly via arachnoid granulations into the dural venous sinuses.

q: CSF passes from the third ventricle to the fourth ventricle through which structure?
why: Lateral ventricles → foramina of Monro → third ventricle → cerebral aqueduct → fourth ventricle → foramen of Magendie (median) and foramina of Luschka (lateral) → subarachnoid space. Aqueduct stenosis causes non-communicating hydrocephalus.

q: Which superficial vein runs along the lateral (radial) side of the forearm and arm, ending in the axillary vein?
why: The cephalic vein runs laterally and pierces the clavipectoral fascia in the deltopectoral groove to join the axillary vein. The basilic vein runs medially and becomes the axillary vein at the lower border of teres major; it is a common PICC route.

q: Before radial artery cannulation, what does the modified Allen test assess?
o: Brachial artery patency above the elbow
Ulnar collateral flow to the hand
Median nerve integrity at the wrist
why: Both arteries are occluded, the hand blanched, then ulnar pressure released; return of colour within about 5–10 s suggests adequate ulnar collateral flow via the palmar arches. Its predictive value for ischaemia is poor, but it is still widely taught.

q: Which structures pass through the interscalene triangle between scalenus anterior and medius?
o: Vagus nerve and common carotid artery
why: The brachial plexus and subclavian artery pass between scalenus anterior and medius over the first rib. The subclavian vein passes anterior to scalenus anterior, and the phrenic nerve runs on its anterior surface.

q: A cervical rib most commonly compresses which nerve roots in thoracic outlet syndrome?
why: Neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome usually affects the lower trunk (C8–T1), causing ulnar-sided paraesthesia and wasting of the small hand muscles. Vascular compression of the subclavian artery or vein is less common.

q: Which part of a long bone in a growing child contains the growth plate?
why: Longitudinal growth occurs at the physis (epiphyseal plate) between the epiphysis and the metaphysis. The metaphysis is highly vascular, which is relevant to intraosseous access sites and to osteomyelitis in children.

q: What is the recommended first-choice site for intraosseous access in a child?
o: Distal radius just above the wrist crease
Sternum in the midline at the angle of Louis
Anteromedial proximal tibia below the tuberosity
Anterior iliac crest near the ASIS
Proximal femoral shaft below the trochanter
why: The anteromedial proximal tibia is flat and has a thin cortex. Alternatives include the distal tibia above the medial malleolus, distal femur and, in adults, the proximal humerus. The sternum is used only with specific devices in adults.

q: Which branch of the vagus nerve supplies the cricothyroid muscle?
why: The superior laryngeal nerve divides into the internal (sensory above the cords) and external (motor to cricothyroid) branches. The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies all other intrinsic laryngeal muscles and sensation below the cords.

q: The vagus nerve leaves the skull through which foramen?
why: CN X exits through the jugular foramen with IX and XI, then descends in the carotid sheath between the internal jugular vein and the carotid artery.

q: In a TAP block, local anaesthetic is deposited in the plane between which two muscles?
o: Rectus abdominis and posterior rectus sheath
why: The thoracolumbar nerves (T6–L1) run between internal oblique and transversus abdominis. A lateral TAP covers roughly T10–T12; a subcostal approach covers higher dermatomes. The rectus sheath block targets the plane posterior to rectus abdominis.

q: Below the arcuate line, what forms the posterior wall of the rectus sheath?
o: Aponeuroses of internal oblique and transversus abdominis
why: Above the arcuate line the posterior sheath is formed by the posterior lamina of internal oblique and transversus abdominis aponeuroses. Below it, all aponeuroses pass anterior to rectus, leaving only transversalis fascia (and peritoneum) behind.

sb: The Hip Joint & Fascia Iliaca Compartment
q: In a fascia iliaca compartment block, local anaesthetic is placed deep to the fascia iliaca and superficial to which muscle?
why: The femoral and lateral femoral cutaneous nerves (and variably obturator) run beneath the fascia iliaca on the iliopsoas. Volume-dependent spread within this compartment is used for hip fracture analgesia (suprainguinal approach gives better proximal spread).

sb: The Hip Joint & Fascia Iliaca Compartment
q: Which nerves supply the anterior hip joint capsule and are targeted by a PENG block?
o: Sciatic nerve and superior gluteal nerve
Femoral nerve, obturator nerve and accessory obturator nerve
Lateral femoral cutaneous and genitofemoral nerves
why: The anterior hip capsule is innervated by articular branches of the femoral, obturator and accessory obturator nerves. The PENG (pericapsular nerve group) block deposits LA between the iliopsoas tendon and the pubic ramus near the iliopubic eminence.

q: How many nerves are blocked in a complete ankle block?
why: Five: tibial, deep peroneal, superficial peroneal, sural and saphenous. The tibial and deep peroneal nerves are deep (beneath fascia); the others are superficial and blocked by subcutaneous infiltration.

q: Where is the deep peroneal nerve blocked at the ankle?
o: Behind the lateral malleolus beside the short saphenous vein
Beside the dorsalis pedis artery between EHL and EDL
Behind the medial malleolus with the tibial artery
Over the medial malleolus beside the saphenous vein
why: The deep peroneal nerve lies alongside the dorsalis pedis artery between the EHL and EDL tendons, supplying the first web space. The tibial nerve lies behind the posterior tibial artery posterior to the medial malleolus; the sural nerve lies behind the lateral malleolus.

sb: The Heart — Innervation & Coronary Blood Flow
q: When does most left ventricular coronary blood flow occur?
why: High intramural pressure during systole compresses subendocardial vessels, so about 80% of LV flow occurs in diastole. Coronary perfusion pressure is aortic diastolic pressure minus LVEDP, and tachycardia shortens diastole, reducing supply.

sb: The Heart — Innervation & Coronary Blood Flow
q: Into which chamber does the coronary sinus drain?
why: The coronary sinus runs in the posterior atrioventricular groove and opens into the right atrium between the IVC and the tricuspid valve, guarded by the Thebesian valve. Thebesian veins drain directly into chambers, contributing to the physiological shunt.

q: Which muscle elevates the upper eyelid and is supplied by the oculomotor nerve?
why: Levator palpebrae superioris (CN III) elevates the lid; Müller's muscle (sympathetic) adds about 2 mm, explaining the mild ptosis in Horner's syndrome. Orbicularis oculi (CN VII) closes the eye.

q: What is the nerve supply to the lateral rectus muscle?
why: LR6 SO4, all the rest 3: lateral rectus (CN VI), superior oblique (CN IV), and the other extraocular muscles (CN III). Raised ICP can cause a false-localising sixth nerve palsy because of its long intracranial course.

q: Calot's triangle, dissected during cholecystectomy, is bordered by the cystic duct, the common hepatic duct and which other structure?
o: The inferior border of the liver
why: Calot's (hepatobiliary) triangle is bounded by the cystic duct, common hepatic duct and the inferior surface of the liver. It contains the cystic artery, usually from the right hepatic artery.

q: Why may gallbladder pain be referred to the right shoulder tip?
o: Phrenic nerve irritation via the diaphragm (C3–C5)
Stimulation of the T7 dermatome via splanchnic nerves
Vagus nerve irritation via the hepatic plexus
Compression of the axillary nerve by the liver
Irritation of the brachial plexus at the thoracic outlet
why: Inflammation irritating the diaphragm is carried by the phrenic nerve (C3–C5), and pain is referred to the C4 dermatome over the shoulder. Visceral gallbladder pain is carried in sympathetic fibres (T6–T9) to the epigastrium and right upper quadrant. The same mechanism explains shoulder tip pain after laparoscopy.

q: Which structure lies in the superior mediastinum?
why: The superior mediastinum contains the aortic arch and its branches, SVC and brachiocephalic veins, trachea, oesophagus, thymus, thoracic duct, vagus and phrenic nerves, and the left recurrent laryngeal nerve.

q: An anterior mediastinal mass is most dangerous during induction of anaesthesia because of which mechanism?
o: Phrenic nerve palsy prevents diaphragmatic movement
Pulmonary vascular resistance rises with hypoxia
Induction removes tone that splints the airway and vessels open
Chest wall rigidity increases after induction
why: In the awake, upright patient, muscle tone and negative intrathoracic pressure keep the airways and vessels open. Induction, paralysis and supine positioning can cause tracheobronchial or SVC/pulmonary artery collapse. Plans include awake techniques, maintaining spontaneous ventilation and ECMO standby.

q: Which connective tissue layer surrounds individual nerve fascicles?
why: Endoneurium surrounds individual axons, perineurium surrounds fascicles (and forms the blood–nerve barrier), and epineurium surrounds the whole nerve. Intrafascicular injection (inside perineurium) carries the highest risk of nerve injury.

q: Which fibre type is the most sensitive to local anaesthetic block (blocked first)?
why: Small myelinated B fibres are blocked first, then C and A-delta (pain, temperature), then A-beta (touch), then A-alpha (motor). This explains the higher sympathetic block level than sensory level in neuraxial anaesthesia.

q: Which nerve supplies sensation to the palmar surface of the thumb, index and middle fingers?
why: The median nerve supplies the palmar lateral three and a half digits (and their nail beds). The ulnar nerve supplies the medial one and a half digits; the radial nerve supplies the dorsum of the lateral hand and first web space.

q: Which nerve supplies most of the intrinsic muscles of the hand?
why: The ulnar nerve supplies the interossei, medial two lumbricals, hypothenar muscles, adductor pollicis and deep head of flexor pollicis brevis. The median nerve supplies the 'LOAF' muscles: lateral two lumbricals, opponens pollicis, abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis (superficial head).

q: In Seddon's classification, which injury involves axonal disruption with intact connective tissue sheaths, allowing good recovery by regeneration?
why: Neurapraxia is a conduction block without axonal loss (recovers in weeks). Axonotmesis disrupts axons but preserves the endoneurium so regeneration (about 1 mm/day) is guided. Neurotmesis divides the whole nerve and usually needs surgical repair.

q: Which nerve is most commonly injured by positioning during general anaesthesia?
why: The ulnar nerve is the most frequently reported perioperative nerve injury, from compression at the cubital tunnel, especially with the forearm pronated. Keeping the forearm supinated or neutral and padding the elbow reduce risk. The common peroneal nerve is at risk in lithotomy at the fibular head.

q: Approximately how far from the incisor teeth is the oesophagogastric junction in an adult?
why: The oesophagus begins about 15 cm from the incisors (C6), is about 25 cm long and the gastro-oesophageal junction lies about 40 cm from the incisors (T11). This guides placement of oesophageal temperature and Doppler probes.

q: Which statement about the lower oesophageal sphincter is correct?
o: Barrier pressure is LOS pressure minus gastric pressure
It is an anatomical sphincter of skeletal muscle
Its tone is increased by suxamethonium-induced fasciculations only
why: The LOS is a physiological sphincter, aided by the crural diaphragm. Barrier pressure (LOS minus intragastric pressure) protects against reflux. Anticholinergics, opioids, propofol and volatiles reduce LOS tone; metoclopramide, neostigmine and suxamethonium increase it (suxamethonium raises gastric pressure as well).

q: In a peribulbar block, why is the needle directed inferotemporally?
o: To reach the ciliary ganglion directly in the cone
To deposit LA into the lacrimal gland
To avoid the optic nerve and superomedial vessels
To block the facial nerve to orbicularis oculi
To enter the cone through the superior rectus
why: The inferotemporal quadrant is relatively avascular and away from the superior oblique trochlea and the medial vessels. Peribulbar blocks stay extraconal; retrobulbar (intraconal) blocks carry greater risk of globe perforation, optic nerve injury and brainstem anaesthesia.

q: Which structure passes through the optic canal?
why: The optic canal transmits CN II and the ophthalmic artery. The superior orbital fissure transmits III, IV, V1 branches (lacrimal, frontal, nasociliary), VI and the superior ophthalmic vein.

q: Why is pain from the parietal pleura well localised, but visceral pleura insensitive to pain?
o: Visceral pleura has somatic innervation; parietal has none
Visceral pleura is supplied by the phrenic nerves
Parietal pleura has no nerve supply of its own
Both layers are supplied only by the vagus nerve
Parietal pleura has somatic nerves; visceral has autonomic only
why: Parietal pleura receives somatic intercostal nerves (costal) and phrenic nerves (central diaphragmatic and mediastinal, referred to the shoulder). Visceral pleura receives autonomic fibres only and is insensitive to pain.

q: In the mid-axillary line, how far inferiorly does the parietal pleura extend?
why: The pleural reflection lies at rib 8 in the midclavicular line, rib 10 in the midaxillary line and rib 12 posteriorly (about two ribs below the lung edge at each line). The pleura also rises 2–3 cm above the medial clavicle.

q: Which nerve is NOT one of the sensory nerves blocked in a scalp block?
why: Scalp block targets the supraorbital, supratrochlear, zygomaticotemporal, auriculotemporal, greater, lesser and third occipital nerves (and great auricular). The facial nerve is motor to the face and is not a target.

q: When blocking the auriculotemporal nerve for a scalp block, which vessel lies close to the injection point?
why: The auriculotemporal nerve is blocked about 1–1.5 cm anterior to the tragus at the level of the tragus, beside the superficial temporal artery, which should be palpated and avoided. The greater occipital nerve lies medial to the occipital artery.

q: The portal vein is formed by the union of which veins?
o: Superior mesenteric and inferior vena cava
why: The portal vein forms behind the neck of the pancreas from the superior mesenteric and splenic veins (the inferior mesenteric usually drains into the splenic). It supplies about 75% of liver blood flow but about half of its oxygen supply.

q: Which is a site of portosystemic anastomosis that can produce varices in portal hypertension?
why: Portosystemic anastomoses: lower oesophagus (left gastric/azygos), anorectal (superior/middle and inferior rectal), umbilical (paraumbilical/epigastric, caput medusae) and retroperitoneal. Oesophageal varices are the most clinically important.

q: In a supine patient, aspirated material most commonly enters which segment?
o: Superior (apical) segment of right lower lobe
Apical segment of right upper lobe
Anterior basal segment of left lower lobe
why: In the supine position, the posterior segment of the right upper lobe and the superior segment of the right lower lobe are dependent. When upright, aspirate tends to go to the right lower lobe basal segments.

q: Approximately how many generations of airway division are there from the trachea to the alveolar sacs?
why: Weibel's model describes 23 generations: the conducting zone (generations 0–16, anatomical dead space about 150 mL) and the respiratory zone (17–23, respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts and sacs).

q: Which division of the trigeminal nerve carries motor fibres?
why: Only the mandibular division (V3) has a motor root, supplying the muscles of mastication, mylohyoid, anterior belly of digastric, tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini.

q: Trigeminal neuralgia most often affects which division(s)?
o: Ophthalmic and maxillary equally with the ophthalmic commonest
why: Trigeminal neuralgia most often involves V2 and/or V3; isolated V1 involvement is uncommon (under 5%). Carbamazepine is first-line; microvascular decompression treats vascular compression at the root entry zone.

q: Which hormone is released from the posterior pituitary?
why: The posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis) releases ADH and oxytocin, made in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus. The anterior pituitary releases GH, prolactin, ACTH, TSH, FSH and LH.

q: A pituitary macroadenoma compressing the optic chiasm classically produces which visual field defect?
why: Crossing nasal retinal fibres at the chiasm carry temporal field information, so central compression gives bitemporal hemianopia, often starting in the upper temporal quadrants because the tumour grows from below. Optic tract lesions cause homonymous defects.
